newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-PETTITTE, KEY TO START FIRST TWO FOR YANKS IN SERIES.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-PETTITTE, KEY TO START FIRST TWO FOR YANKS IN SERIES.

text.p: New York Yankees manager Joe Torre said Friday that he would start left-handers Andy Pettitte and Jimmy Key against the Atlanta Braves in the first two games of the World Series.
Against the defending champions' power from the left side, Torre said, "I felt that I wanted to go left-handed."

Looming over the scheduled Saturday opener of the best-of-seven Series is a forecast for possible heavy rain and wind. A rainout would push Game 1 to Sunday and Game 2 to Monday, leaving no off-day before Games 3, 4 and 5 in Atlanta.
"If we're rained out tomorrow it can only help the Braves," said Torre.

The National League champions had only one day off after clinching Thursday night, so Atlanta manager Bobby Cox would have little flexibility in his pitching rotation if the Series opened as scheduled Saturday.
In the event of a rainout, said Torre, "If Bobby wants to make some alterations he can do that."

The Braves come in having outscored the St Louis Cardinals 32-1 over the final three games of the National League Championship Series, finishing with an astonishing 15-0 win to complete a recovery from a three games to one deficit.
"They're hot," said Yankee shortstop Derek Jeter. "To be honest, when they were down 3-1 I still thought they'd win."
Said Pettitte: "The Braves are playing unbelievable right now. I'm hoping they used up all their hits and runs."
Torre said he had not had a chance to talk with his assistant coaches about how slugger Darryl Strawberry, who has a fracture in his right big toe, had looked in practice.

Strawberry, who had tape wrapped around his right shoe to hold a pad in place over his toes, appeared to run fairly well in the outfield and was reaching the upper decks with some of his practice swings.
Torre wants Strawberry in left field if at all possible.
"If he can move around and be able to play the outfield I anticipate him being out there."

And what happens to designated hitter Cecil Fielder when the Series moves to the National League city, where the designated hitter rule is not in effect? Torre ruled out putting the big-hitting Fielder in at first base.
"Tino Martinez is my first baseman," said Torre. "I'm just going to have a pretty good bench in Atlanta."
Moving Key to the second start bumps right-hander David Cone to the number three spot.
But Pettitte pointed out that lefty pitchers do not always have the advantage over lefty batters.
"I've really struggled against lefties this year. They've hit better for average than righties this year," he said.
But overall, said Pettitte, "I think it's an advantage for us, definitely."
Torre and pitching coach Mel Stottlemyre had conferred with Pettitte last week to settle him down when he was trying to do too much and had two subpar post-season starts.
Apparently it worked, since Pettitte held the Baltimore Orioles to three hits through eight innings in the American League Championship Series clincher.
Pettitte called the meeting "a little chat to tell me to stay within myself."
Now, he said, he would "try not to get so worked up... I want to enjoy myself a little more."

He said he and Stottlemyre were talking about it again Friday during practice. Now that the Yankees had reached the Series, "The pressure should be over, the pressure should be off," Pettitte said. "I'm going to try to relax."
Relaxation will not be easy for Yankee batters trying to break through against an Atlanta trio of starting pitchers considered the best in baseball.
"You have to think small," Torre said. "They're a little stingy and you have to take what they give you."
Torre noted that unlike past Yankee lineups, his was not really a power-hitting team but one that had to "think one run at a time."
"I think it's going to be a heck of a series and I think it's going to be a low-scoring series if both clubs do what they're supposed to do," Torre predicted.
